query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets that all exhibit a single-phase FCC structure after identical thermomechanical processing, the differences in mechanical behavior during deformation and failure are controlled by variations in local chemical short‐range order and the associated lattice distortion. These factors modulate the stacking fault energy and dislocation mobility such that the full quinary alloy exhibits enhanced dislocation pinning and twinning activity, leading to superior yield strength and work hardening compared to its reduced-component subsets.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets produced under identical thermomechanical conditions
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of alloy composition by selectively removing one or two constituent elements from Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni while keeping processing parameters constant, followed by mechanical deformation testing
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile or compression deformation tests at room temperature (with potential extension to variable strain rates/temperatures) on samples confirmed to be single-phase FCC
generation.structural_mediator: Differences in local chemical short-range order and lattice distortion that affect stacking fault energies and dislocation migration/twinning mechanisms
generation.mechanism: The quinary alloy’s full complement of elements creates larger local lattice distortions and a more complex chemical environment that promotes dislocation pinning and may lower the energy barrier for deformation twinning. In contrast, the removal of one or more elements in quaternary or ternary alloys reduces these local strain fields, leading to lower yield strengths and diminished work hardening despite an identical overall FCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary subsets will show a measurable reduction in yield strength and work hardening rate, with fewer deformation twins under identical deformation conditions due to a more homogeneous local chemical environment and higher effective stacking fault energies.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies only to alloys processed to obtain a single-phase FCC microstructure without secondary precipitates; deviations such as phase separation or significant texture differences would place the system outside the valid domain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of specific elemental interactions to the local short-range order and stacking fault energy are not well established, and direct measurement of these metrics may involve significant experimental uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of samples consisting of the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its corresponding quaternary and ternary subsets, ensuring all samples are processed under identical thermomechanical conditions to yield a single-phase FCC microstructure. Characterize local chemical short-range order via atom probe tomography and measure stacking fault energies by in situ TEM or diffraction techniques. Subject each composition to uniaxial tensile or compression tests while simultaneously recording the onset of dislocation motion and twinning activity.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate from mechanical tests
Density and distribution of deformation twins and dislocation structures via TEM/EBSD
Quantitative assessment of local chemical order (e.g., clustering metrics) using atom probe tomography
Stacking fault energies measured by diffraction or other in situ methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not exhibit significantly higher yield strength, work hardening rate, or enhanced twinning compared to the quaternary and ternary subsets—or if measurements reveal comparable levels of local chemical ordering and similar stacking fault energies across all compositions—the hypothesis would be falsified.

[ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
